title: Westbrook School Committee — School Committee Meeting

fields.Location: Westbrook High School (Room 114), 125 Stroudwater St. (Hybrid via Zoom)

note: This summary highlights the meeting's key discussions and decisions, with timestamps for verification — it is not a substitute for watching the full meeting. The full committee (all seven members) was present; one student representative (Tina Nguyen) was present and delivered the student report. For complete context, nuance, and anything not covered, watch the full video at the link above. (Produced by: WestbrookCurrents.com)
attendance: Present: Chair Andrea Mancuso, Vice Chair Katy Rice, Allison Brunette, Erin Cavallaro, Noreen Poitras, Brooke Reed, Dr. Flynn Ross.

blocks.x: Superintendent's Report: State of the Schools

Dr. Lancia delivered the district's annual State of the Schools presentation (a 60-plus page report posted online), built around this year's theme, “I Belong Here.” As of January 2026, the district serves 2,377 students pre-K through grade 12: 27% in special education (highest share in Cumberland County), 26% multilingual, 3% McKinney-Vento homeless-eligible, and 59% meeting federal low-income guidelines. The district has 496 employees (six positions unfilled). Special education now serves 609 students, up 13 from last year and a 70% increase over the past decade; the Director of Special Education Services position has been vacant all year after two unsuccessful searches. The multilingual program serves 588 students (up 60), with strong ACCESS assessment growth districtwide.

FY26's $53.35 million budget was a lean “maintenance” budget; per-pupil spending ($21,135) is fourth-lowest in Cumberland County, according to the district. Solar panels have been installed at Congin and Saccarappa, with the middle school and high school scheduled for this spring/summer; once operating, the project is estimated to reduce energy costs by about $305,000 a year (a separate figure from the $279,000 Siemens energy-efficiency savings reported March 4). All school kitchens are now halal-certified, and School Nutrition Director Mary Emerson was named Maine's Nutrition Director of the Year for 2025. The district relaunched the Westbrook Education Foundation, and a group of alumni has been forming a new Westbrook High School Alumni Association.

State figures don't support this ranking on total cost. The Maine Department of Education's latest posted data (FY2025) puts Westbrook at $22,291 per pupil, 11th-lowest of 17 Cumberland County districts. The district hasn't said which measure its ranking uses.

Dr. Lancia noted a decrease in chronic absenteeism this year, cautioning that next year's comparison may differ because some students were kept home earlier this year out of fear tied to immigration enforcement; he credited a community-volunteer response during that period and noted the district has since refined its own immigration-enforcement response plan alongside its existing safety protocols.
Board Discussion: Assessments, Per-Pupil Spending & State Funding

Member Erin Cavallaro asked whether state assessments account for a student's first language; Dr. Lancia explained multilingual students get only a one-time exemption from the English language arts test, and that the district relies more on the separate ACCESS assessment to gauge real multilingual progress. Chair Mancuso asked how the district's low per-pupil spending interacts with its unusually complex student population; Dr. Lancia described a deliberately lean, needs-based budget that still tries to remove financial barriers to opportunity even as class sizes creep upward. Dr. Flynn Ross noted the seeming paradox that Westbrook's rising property valuation has simultaneously reduced the district's federal and state funding support. Separately, in her Chair's report, Chair Mancuso said she had met with Governor Mills the day before (at Representative Salisbury's invitation, with Mayor Morse and Sue Joyce of the Chamber) to discuss federal funding challenges and a newly proposed state funding formula.
11.1–11.6 — Six School Department Policy Actions, Final Approval (Taken in the Aggregate)

The same six policy actions first approved February 11 — adopt Policy BID (School Committee Member Compensation), approve Policy EHB, EHB–R2, and EHB–R3, and delete Policy EHB–L and EHB–LR — received final approval as a bloc.
Approved 7–0, moved by Noreen Poitras, seconded by Erin Cavallaro.
12.1 — Teacher Nomination: Special Education Teacher, Westbrook Middle School
A nomination to fill a Special Education Teacher vacancy at Westbrook Middle School, replacing a resigned teacher (per the packet: Sarah Hager, replacing Keith Wixson).
Approved 7–0. Moved by Erin Cavallaro, seconded by Noreen Poitras.

Staff professional-development days August 27–28, students starting Monday, August 31, with kindergarten and Pre-K first days still to be determined because of screening days. There will be no staggered kindergarten/Pre-K start this year; Dr. Lancia said survey feedback urged against repeating the practice, and Dr. O'Donnell described views as mixed, citing childcare challenges. In the same survey, about 78% of staff and 52% of community respondents preferred this calendar overall. The calendar includes 177 student days, two more than Maine's 175-day minimum.
Approved 7–0 (first reading). Moved by Katy Rice, seconded by Dr. Flynn Ross.
